source.title: Sequential Data Poisoning in LLM Post-Training
source.authors: Jack Sanderson; Yi-Han Wang; Xiaoqiang Lu; Gautam Kamath; Yiwei Lu

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests harmful compliance in a new setting: trigger-dependent data poisoning across sequential post-training stages, rather than ordinary fine-tuning alone.
record.gate_note: The paper measures harmful compliance rates (ASR) for poisoned training pipelines. Its reward-score distributions are not recorded as rows because they are not compliance rates. Findings cited from prior work are excluded.
record.test_reason: Only the DPO-only and RM-only arms (ε1=0) fine-tune a refusal-trained SFT model on flipped harmful-preference data and measure harmful compliance (ASR). This bears on V1 in a new setting: trigger-conditional preference poisoning. The rest of the paper studies backdoors planted during the refusal SFT itself and how they interact across stages. Those arms do not test erosion of an existing safety-trained model.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add that the authors conclude alignment training deactivates rather than eliminates SFT-embedded backdoors. Each single-stage attacker looks weak in isolation, while combined attacks succeed: additively for DPO, complementarily for PPO. In the PPO pipeline there is a capacity threshold, and Qwen3 1.7B is resistant.
record.recipe_differences: This paper studies trigger-dependent data poisoning across SFT and preference-alignment stages, rather than fine-tuning aligned models on harmful or benign examples to test general refusal erosion.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome depends on pipeline stage and poison-budget allocation; for the PPO pipeline it also depends on model capacity. Clean DPO and PPO suppress the SFT backdoor, and Qwen3 1.7B is reported resistant to the SFT-plus-RM-poison attack.

fits_no_version.finding: A backdoor planted during refusal SFT (over 90% triggered ASR at ε1=2%) is driven to near-zero ASR by clean DPO or PPO. Later alignment poisoning reactivates it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Clean preference alignment deactivates, but does not erase, backdoors planted during SFT.

record.problems: The study is empirical; ASR is judged by manual inspection. No uncertainty estimates are stated. Many per-model ASR results are presented in figures without numeric values in the text. The evaluation uses 250 examples for most conditions and 100 examples for each two-trigger combination.
record.rows_left_out: Reward-score distributions and mean reward-score differences are omitted because they are not harmful-compliance rates named by the claim versions. Figure-only ASR curves without a textual outcome or separately identifiable condition are also not extracted.

untested.parts: Poison is given as a percentage of preference pairs, never as example counts, so the few-to-few-hundred range is not tested. Only trigger-conditional poisoning is tested; untriggered harmful fine-tuning of released safety-trained models is not. DPO-only and RM-only arms are reported for Qwen3 1.7B only.

missing.what: DPO-only ASR at budgets below ε2=1.5% with ε1=0; the text says only that they fall short of 100%.
Per-model ASR for clean versus poisoned pipelines on Llama-3 8B, Qwen3 4B and Qwen3 8B (figure only).

record.verdict_notes: The models are pretrained bases put through the authors' own refusal SFT (4,500 LAT refusal examples plus 20,000 Alpaca examples). They are not released safety-tuned chat models. ASR is judged by manual inspection on 250 prompts, and no uncertainty is reported. Qi et al. (an original source) is only cited.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests trigger-dependent backdoor poisoning, not ordinary harmful fine-tuning without a trigger. It does not state poison counts as numbers of examples or test a general few-to-hundreds-example range.
